FLIGHT PATH RECONSTRUCTION

This project is built in conjunction with the data scraper project, with the future goal of combining the skills gained and projects completed across these 2 to build a flight controller and ground station for UAV projects. This project takes the recorded flight data and maps the fake sensor readings from warthunder to a reconstructed flight path. A demonstrator is included that shows a small circuit flown by a F18, as well as some aerobatic manouvers (not disimilar to those seen in the new topgun movie).

StatusCompleted TypePersonal project ToolsMATLAB, three.js (browser replay)

Project introduction

The flight data logger records altitude, attitude, heading and airspeed, but not position. This script works out where the aircraft went from those values alone, then replays the flight: the path with the aircraft flying along it, a close-up of its attitude, and plots that draw in as the flight plays. The aim of using only gyroscope, speed, and altitude readings is to replicate realistic simple aircraft sensor availability.

Below is a real 4-minute log, take-off, a short circuit with some aerobatics, and a landing back on the same runway. NOTE; my html and 3.js skills are still developing, resizing the browsr window MAY cause the play and speed buttons to disapear, to avoid, reload the page at your desired window size.

Major design choices

  • Dead reckoning sideways + measured altitude upwards. The horizontal track comes from adding up airspeed along the heading, step by step. Height is taken straight from the logged altitude instead of being integrated, so vertical error can’t build up.
  • Step by step integration. Speed and heading are only known about twice a second, so a higher-order method would add complexity without adding accuracy.
  • Aircraft views: At the scale of the whole flight a 17 m jet is invisible, so the path view uses an enlarged model and a second view shows its attitude up close.
  • Height lines: Vertical lines every 20 samples make height readable in a 3D view that can be rotated to any angle.
  • Sacrificed: wind, sideslip and angle of attack. The aircraft is assumed to move exactly where its nose points. None of these are logged, so they can’t be corrected for, and they matter most in hard manoeuvres. This is further discussed in future developments.

Design

Each step moves the aircraft along its heading \(\psi\) and pitch \(\theta\) at its true airspeed \(V\), then turns the model to the logged attitude.

Airspeed
\[ V_k = \frac{\text{TAS}_k}{3.6} \quad \text{m/s} \]
North and east
\[ \begin{aligned} N_k &= N_{k-1} + V_{k-1}\cos\theta_{k-1}\cos\psi_{k-1}\,\Delta t \\ E_k &= E_{k-1} + V_{k-1}\cos\theta_{k-1}\sin\psi_{k-1}\,\Delta t \end{aligned} \]
Height
\[ Z_k = h_k - h_0 \]
Model attitude
\[ R = R_z(\psi)\,R_y(\theta)\,R_x(\phi) \]
  • Sign conventions: the game’s artificial horizon reports nose-up pitch and right bank as negative, so both are flipped before driving the model and plots.
  • Cleaning the log: one stale sample from before the aircraft spawned (1,030 m at 529 km/h on the runway) is removed, and the parked time before and after the flight is trimmed.
  • Smooth replay: position and attitude are interpolated between samples, with heading and roll taking the short way round across 0°/360° and ±180°.
  • Aircraft model: A F-18 STL file is sourced from 3D modeling community forums, this file can be swapped for any desired aircraft.

Results

  • Lands back on the runway: after 133 s and 15 km in the air, the reconstructed touchdown is 19 m from the take-off runway’s centreline.
  • The flight: Flight data recorded from the previous project is replicated exactly with no errors present, and the simulated flight path is visually extremely similar to what was seen in game.
  • 2.2 samples per second from the logger: 677 samples over 303 s.

Future developments

  • Sub-second timestamps: This would store time as seconds since the start of logging, to the millisecond.
  • Angle of attack and sideslip: Logging these variables would give a more accurate flight path, as the velocity can point along the true flight path rather than the nose, which is particularly relevant for the manovoures in this flight and others in an aircraft with the performance of an F18 which can maintain a very high AOA. This would however, ignore the aim of realistic sensor availability, as measuring AOA and sideslip on a small RC aircraft is difficult and expensive.
  • Real-time playback in MATLAB. Pause by each sample’s time step instead of a fixed 0.1 s, so the replay runs at true speed.
  • Live replay: As this project is used to build towards a UAV groundstation project, a liuve replay will more closely replicate what this future project will aim to achieve.
